title: The Services Nobody Notices Until They Fail: Water, Waste, Lifts, Light, Sound and Safety
summary: Building services are the systems an occupant judges the building by every day: water pressure, a drain that never backs up, an elevator that arrives, a quiet bedroom and a lobby that feels safe. Each is decided early, by space and by layout, long before anyone picks a fixture. Felix, Noor and Silas set the frame.
body:
Occupants never praise a building service. They judge the building by its failures: the shower that runs weak on the top floor, the elevator wait, the neighbour heard through the wall, the dark path to the car park. Every one of those is decided by space and layout early, and almost none can be fixed cheaply later.

Recall

Q. What does a dedicated outdoor air system do?

A. It conditions and dries all incoming fresh air centrally, so the room units only handle heat. In a humid climate it is the main defence against cool, damp rooms.

Q. Why does the vapour control layer usually sit toward the outside of a wall in a hot-humid climate?

A. Because moisture drives from the hot, humid exterior toward the cooler, drier interior, and the layer must stop it before it reaches a cold surface where it can condense.

Q. What is a stage gate in design management?

A. A formal review at the end of a design stage where the owner checks the design against the brief, cost and programme, and decides whether to proceed, revise or stop.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, building services decide how a building feels to live in and how it is reviewed, rented and resold. Noor, who leads lighting and acoustics, and Silas, who leads security, join me today because their work and mine compete for the same space: the core, the ceiling void and the ground floor. If you understand what each service needs early, you can protect it at the stage gates instead of losing it to the next value-engineering list.

Water in and water out

In plain English: the city supplies water at a pressure that may not reach your top floor, so you may need to store it and pump it up. Waste leaves by gravity, so it needs slope and a route.

The professional framing has three parts. Domestic water arrives from the utility main, often through a meter and a backflow preventer that stops building water flowing back into the public supply. If the main pressure cannot reach the highest fixture with enough residual pressure, a booster pump set raises it, often in zones so lower floors are not over-pressured. Where the public supply is unreliable, a storage tank gives the building hours or days of autonomy, sized against how long an interruption you want to survive. Stored water must be kept moving and at safe temperatures, a point Ford takes up tomorrow.

Wastewater, the sanitary drainage, runs down stacks and across the lowest level to the public sewer, or to an on-site treatment system where there is none. Stormwater, the rain off roofs and paving, is a separate system. Many authorities now limit how fast you may release it, so it is held back in a detention tank or a landscaped basin and let out slowly. Each of these takes physical space, and the tanks are heavy, so they shape the structure Bram designed.

A worked example, hypothetical. A 12-storey residential tower on a supply that runs at low pressure at peak hours. The engineer proposes a ground-level storage tank holding a day's demand and a booster set with two pumps, each able to carry the full load, so one can fail or be serviced. The owner's decision is the autonomy: one day, or three. Day 5 works that out.

Vertical transport

In plain English: elevators are a queue problem. Too few, too slow or too small, and the building feels broken twice a day.

The professional framing is traffic analysis. An elevator consultant estimates the morning peak, the interval between cars arriving, and handling capacity, which is the share of the building's population the elevators can move in a five-minute peak. Car speed, size, door times and the number of stops all matter. In the United States, elevator design, installation, inspection and testing follow ASME A17.1, the Safety Code for Elevators and Escalators, as adopted by the state or city, which usually also licenses the inspectors. The building code adds requirements such as accessible car sizes and, in taller buildings, fire service access elevators. Verify against the current adopted edition.

A second worked example, hypothetical. A 150-unit building with one elevator meets a minimum, but when that elevator is out for service, residents with prams, wheelchairs or groceries face the stairs, and a move-in day blocks everyone. A second car costs money and core space; it also buys redundancy. That is the same choice as the critical-loads list from last week, in a different system.

Say that out loud now.

Every service needs space and a route, decided early. One of anything is a single point of failure.

Light, sound and safety

Noor's point is that lighting and acoustics are product, not decoration. Good lighting design meets the energy code's limits and still lights faces, paths and signs well; bad lighting meets the code and makes a corridor feel like a car park. Acoustics is mostly mass, separation and airtightness: walls and floors between homes must meet minimum sound ratings in the building code, and the complaints come from the gaps, such as a shared duct, a pipe penetration or a hard floor laid on a slab without an underlay.

Silas's point is that security begins with design, not cameras. Crime prevention through environmental design, called CPTED, uses sight lines, lighting, clear boundaries and natural surveillance from windows and active ground floors so that a space feels watched and owned. Access control and cameras then support a design that already works, rather than compensating for one that does not.

A third worked example, hypothetical, that joins Noor's and Silas's points. A ground-floor lobby with a long, dim corridor to the parking entrance and a mail room tucked out of sight. Noor would light the route evenly, with light on faces rather than glare in eyes. Silas would open a sight line from the lobby desk to the parking door and put the mail room where people pass. Neither change costs much at concept; both are expensive after the walls are built.

How the best do it

Disciplined owners protect services space before the architecture hardens. They fix the core size, riser locations, plant rooms, tank volumes and ceiling depths at concept, with each specialist signing a short space allocation sheet. A small developer can copy this with one page per service listing the space it needs and the stage by which it must be confirmed.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: elevators and services equipment may be classed separately from the structure for depreciation in some systems; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Liability: water-borne illness, an elevator injury or a crime in a poorly lit space are all claims against the owner. Banking: lenders and insurers ask about water autonomy, elevator redundancy and security. Governance: name who owns each service's maintenance regime after handover. Estate: long-lived equipment with service contracts is easier for successors to hold. Exit: buyers inspect elevators and water systems, and a poor maintenance record reduces the price.

Professional sign-off required: licensed plumbing or mechanical engineer; elevator consultant; acoustic consultant; security consultant; civil engineer for stormwater.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is losing services space at an early stage gate, when it looks like empty area, and discovering later that tanks, risers or a second elevator no longer fit. The control is a signed space allocation for every service at concept, protected at each gate.

The beginner's mistake

Choosing services by catalogue at the end. The beginner thinks of elevators, pumps and lights as products to buy. The professional thinks of them as space, routes and redundancy to plan.

Callback

In Week 101, Cyrus taught accessible routes and accessible units. An accessible unit on the tenth floor is only accessible while an elevator runs. Elevator redundancy is therefore an accessibility decision as well as a convenience one, and it belongs in the same review.

Recap

Water needs pressure, storage and backflow protection; waste and stormwater need routes, slope and sometimes detention. Elevators are a queue problem governed by ASME A17.1 as adopted. Lighting and acoustics are product. Security starts with design. Every service needs space decided early.

Next: Ford, on Failure Forensics: the Legionnaires' disease outbreak in the South Bronx in 2015.
checklist: Every service has a signed space allocation at concept.
I know the utility pressure and whether a booster set and zoning are needed.
I have chosen the water autonomy period on purpose.
Stormwater release limits have been confirmed with the authority.
An elevator traffic analysis has been done, and redundancy considered.
Acoustic separations and penetrations are detailed, not just rated.
Security design starts with sight lines, lighting and boundaries.
Each service has a named owner for maintenance after handover.
head: Field checklist
speak: Occupants judge a building by its services: water pressure, drains, elevators, quiet and safety. Each is decided by space and layout early. Water may need storage and a booster pump set to reach the top floor, with backflow protection and a choice of how many hours or days of autonomy. Waste runs by gravity, so it needs slope and a route, and stormwater often must be held back and released slowly. Elevators are a queue problem, analysed by a consultant and governed by ASME A17.1 as adopted locally; one elevator is a single point of failure, and that matters for accessibility too. Lighting and acoustics are product: sound complaints come from gaps and penetrations. Security starts with design, through sight lines, lighting and clear boundaries, before cameras. My job is to protect the space every service needs at concept, in writing, and defend it at every stage gate.
terms: Booster pump set — pumps that raise water pressure so that upper floors receive enough flow, often with a duty and a standby pump.
Handling capacity — the share of a building's population its elevators can move in a five-minute peak.
CPTED — crime prevention through environmental design: using sight lines, lighting, boundaries and natural surveillance to reduce crime.

hostile.q: One elevator meets the code. Why does your budget carry two?
hostile.a: Because one elevator is a single point of failure. When it is out for service or a move-in, residents with mobility needs on upper floors cannot reach their homes, which is an accessibility and reputation problem as well as a convenience one. Our traffic analysis also shows the peak wait with one car is longer than our requirements allow. The second car is priced, the core was sized for it at concept, and it is on the space allocation sheet signed at the first stage gate.

title: Water That Sat Still: The South Bronx Legionnaires' Outbreak, 2015
summary: In the summer of 2015 an outbreak of Legionnaires' disease in the South Bronx sickened more than a hundred people and killed a number of them. Health authorities traced it to a building cooling tower. The lesson for an owner is that water systems are a hazard to be managed, not a utility that runs itself.
rule: Rule 106: Every water system in a building you own gets a written water management plan, with a named owner, monitoring, and response triggers; warm or stagnant water is a hazard to manage, never a reserve to forget.
body:
Nothing broke. The pumps ran, the tower cooled the building, the tanks held water. The hazard was biology growing in warm, still water that nobody was measuring, and it reached the street through the air.

Recall

Q. What is a booster pump set, and why does it often have two pumps?

A. Pumps that raise water pressure to reach upper floors. Two pumps, each able to carry the load, let one fail or be serviced without losing supply.

Q. What does Rule 105 require?

A. That every critical function's backup power is decided in writing, with run time and testing, and confirmed on the one-line diagram.

Q. What is clash detection in building information modelling?

A. Automated checking of a combined three-dimensional model to find places where elements of different disciplines, such as a duct and a beam, occupy the same space.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, every building you own will store water somewhere: in tanks, in hot-water heaters, in long pipe runs to rooms that sit empty, and in cooling towers if the plant uses them. Water that sits warm and still can grow Legionella, the bacterium that causes Legionnaires' disease, a serious pneumonia people catch by breathing in fine droplets. That makes water an owner's liability, not just an engineer's design problem.

I will keep to facts that were widely reported by public health authorities. Where I am unsure of a figure, I will describe it without the number. Check the public record before you quote this case.

1. Timeline

In July 2015, New York City health officials identified a cluster of Legionnaires' disease cases in the South Bronx. Over the following weeks the number of cases rose past a hundred, and a number of people died. Investigators tested cooling towers across the area and traced the outbreak strain to a cooling tower at a hotel. Towers that tested positive were disinfected. In August 2015 the city passed a law requiring cooling towers to be registered, inspected and maintained to defined standards, and the state adopted rules of its own. The same year, ASHRAE published Standard 188, on managing the risk of Legionella in building water systems. Verify the current requirements against the primary source before you rely on them.

2. Key decisions

The decisive choices were maintenance choices, made long before the outbreak: how often the tower was cleaned, how its water treatment was dosed and checked, and whether anyone tested for bacteria at all. Before the new law, much of this was left to each owner's judgment. A cooling tower can be operated safely; it can also be run for years on a vague service contract that nobody reads.

3. Assumptions

The hidden assumption, common across many owners, was that a system that works mechanically is safe biologically. A cooling tower that rejects heat well can still be growing bacteria. A second assumption was that treatment chemicals added by a contractor meant the water was controlled, without anyone checking results. A third was that the risk was inside the building, when a cooling tower's drift, the fine mist it releases, carries the risk to people on the street who never entered.

4. Incentives

Testing, cleaning and treatment cost money every month and produce nothing visible. An owner judged on operating cost has a quiet reason to stretch intervals. A service contractor paid per visit has no reason to recommend more scrutiny unless the contract demands it. Nobody in that chain is rewarded for a test result that says the water is fine. Regulation changed the incentive by making the duty explicit and inspected.

5. Warning signs ignored

Legionnaires' outbreaks linked to cooling towers had been documented for decades before 2015. Warm summer weather, which raises tower water temperature, is a known risk factor every year. Warning signs inside any building are measurable: water temperatures in the range where the bacterium grows, low disinfectant levels, scale and biofilm in the tower basin. Without a plan that required these readings, they went unseen.

Say that out loud now.

A water system can work mechanically and still be dangerous biologically. I measure it, or I do not know.

6. Point of no return

For the people who fell ill, the point of no return came when contaminated drift reached the street in hot weather. For the owners, it came earlier, every month that the tower ran without a plan and without testing, because once bacteria are established in a system, the response is an emergency disinfection under public scrutiny rather than routine control.

7. Root cause

The root cause was treating water systems as plant that runs itself rather than as a managed hazard with a written plan, a named owner and measured results. The engineering to control Legionella was well understood. The management system to apply it, consistently, was missing, and the duty fell between owner, operator and service contractor.

Applying it to your projects

Two worked examples, hypothetical. First, an apart-hotel with a large rooftop storage tank and long hot-water runs to rooms that may sit empty for days. Stored water that sits warm and still is exactly the condition to avoid. The design response is a tank sized for the autonomy you need and no larger, hot water stored and circulated hot enough to discourage growth while protecting guests from scalding with mixing valves near the fixtures, and a routine for flushing outlets in vacant rooms. The management response is a water management plan following a recognised standard such as ASHRAE 188, naming who measures what, how often, and what triggers action.

Second, a residential building with a cooling tower. Before you accept the plant, you decide whether a dry cooler or an air-cooled system would avoid a tower altogether, accepting some loss of efficiency in exchange for removing the hazard. If you keep the tower, its treatment, testing, registration and records are written into the operator's contract, and the results come to you, not only to the contractor.

Notice the pattern from last week. Rule 105 made the backup-power decision explicit. Rule 106 does the same for water: a decision about a hazard, written down, owned and measured, rather than left to the default of whoever services the plant.

One more practical point. A water management plan is written for a building, not copied from a template. It starts with a walk of the systems: where water enters, where it is stored, heated, cooled, misted or left standing, and which occupants are most vulnerable. Then it sets control limits for each point, such as a temperature band or a disinfectant level, a method and frequency of checking, and a corrective action when a reading falls outside. Finally it assigns a team and a review date. A plan that cannot name the specific tank, the specific readings and the specific person is not yet a plan.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a building water system with no plan and no measurements, run on a service contract nobody reads. The control is a water management plan at handover, with monitoring results reported to the owner every month.

The beginner's mistake

Oversizing water storage for comfort. A tank twice the size you need is twice as long for water to sit still. Size storage for a chosen autonomy, and design it to turn over.

Professional sign-off required: licensed plumbing or mechanical engineer for design; a water treatment specialist and the operator for the water management plan; legal counsel on registration and reporting duties in your jurisdiction.

Callback

In Week 82, Vera taught contemporaneous records. A water management plan is worthless without the log of readings behind it. If an outbreak is ever investigated, the first request will be for the temperature and disinfectant records, dated and signed. Keep them as if they will be read by an investigator, because one day they may be.

Recap

The 2015 South Bronx outbreak was traced to a building cooling tower. Mechanically sound water systems can grow Legionella when water is warm and still. The root cause was management, not engineering. Rule 106 requires a written water management plan for every system, with an owner, monitoring and triggers.

Next: Nadia, on The Money: what building services do to operating cost, service charges and value.
checklist: Every water system has a written water management plan at handover.
The plan names who measures what, how often, and what triggers action.
Monitoring results come to me every month, not only to the contractor.
Storage is sized for a chosen autonomy and designed to turn over.
Hot water is stored and circulated hot, with scald protection at fixtures.
Vacant rooms have a flushing routine.
I have asked whether the plant can avoid a cooling tower.
Registration and reporting duties have been checked for my jurisdiction.
head: Field checklist
speak: In July 2015, New York City identified a cluster of Legionnaires' disease cases in the South Bronx. Cases passed a hundred and a number of people died. Investigators traced the outbreak to a building cooling tower, and the city then required cooling towers to be registered, inspected and maintained. Legionella grows in warm, still water and spreads in fine droplets, so a tower's mist can reach people on the street. Nothing broke mechanically. The root cause was management: water systems treated as plant that runs itself rather than as a hazard with a plan, an owner and measured results. My rule: every water system in a building I own gets a written water management plan, with a named owner, monitoring and response triggers. I size storage for a chosen autonomy so water turns over, keep hot water hot with scald protection, flush vacant rooms and get the readings every month.
terms: Legionella — a bacterium that grows in warm, still water and causes Legionnaires' disease when fine contaminated droplets are inhaled.
Water management plan — a written programme identifying where a building's water can become hazardous, how it is controlled and monitored, and what triggers action.
Drift — the fine mist of water droplets released from a cooling tower into the surrounding air.

hostile.q: Your operator handles water treatment. Why should I, as your insurer, need to see your water management plan?
hostile.a: Because the liability for water-borne illness is mine as owner, whoever does the work. We have a written plan following a recognised standard. It names who takes temperature and disinfectant readings, how often, and what level triggers flushing or disinfection. The results come to me monthly, and I can give you the last twelve months of logs. We also sized storage to turn over and avoided a cooling tower where the plant allowed it.

title: Services Are a Subscription: Contracts, Charges and the Value of Good Design
summary: Building services are paid for twice: once to install and then every month through service contracts, energy and staffing. Design choices such as security layout or elevator count change those monthly costs for decades. Learn how services flow through the operating budget, the common charges and the accounts, and how to value a design that lowers them.
body:
Every building service is a subscription you sign at design and pay until you sell. Good services design does not just cost less to run; it changes which costs exist at all, and that is where the value is.

Recall

Q. What does Rule 106 require?

A. That every water system in a building you own has a written water management plan with a named owner, monitoring and response triggers.

Q. What are the three buckets for pricing an MEP option?

A. Capital cost to install, operating cost each year, and the replacement reserve for when the equipment wears out.

Q. What is capitalisation in owner accounting?

A. Recording a cost as part of an asset on the balance sheet, to be expensed over its life, rather than as an expense in the year it is paid. The rules differ by accounting framework and tax system.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, an operating budget for a residential or hospitality building is dominated by a short list: staff, energy, insurance, property tax, repairs and service contracts. Building services touch nearly all of them. When a buyer's analyst reads your operating statement, the services lines are where they look for costs that will rise, contracts that lock you in and equipment near the end of its life. You want to know those numbers better than they do.

Where services show up in the accounts

In plain English: running and servicing equipment is an expense each year; replacing a major piece of it is usually an investment in the asset.

The professional framing separates three flows. Service contracts, routine maintenance, energy and staff are operating expenses, deducted before net operating income (NOI). Major replacements, such as modernising an elevator or replacing a booster pump set, are usually capitalised and depreciated, though the threshold and treatment depend on your accounting framework and tax system; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. And a replacement reserve, as Sage taught last week, is the money you set aside for those future capital items, whose place above or below NOI is a lender's convention, not a standard.

In a condominium, the same costs flow to the owners' association as common charges, funded by monthly fees, with a reserve fund for future replacements. A developer who designs expensive-to-run services hands that bill to the buyers, and in many places the disclosure documents must show it. High common charges depress sale prices just as high operating costs depress a rental building's value.

Worked example: security by design or by staffing

Hypothetical round numbers. A 150-unit rental building. Layout A has a deep lobby with blind corners, a hidden mail room and a separate unwatched parking entrance. The security consultant advises a staffed desk around the clock, which, covering every hour of the week with relief and holidays, needs about 4 full-time equivalents at a hypothetical 50,000 dollars each, all-in. That is 200,000 dollars a year.

Layout B applies the crime prevention through environmental design principles Silas taught on Day 1: one controlled entrance with sight lines from the street and the lobby, the mail room beside the entrance, the parking door visible from the desk, good lighting and an access-control system. The consultant advises a staffed desk only in the evening, about 2 full-time equivalents, plus 20,000 dollars a year for the access-control and camera service contract. Annual cost: 120,000 dollars.

The saving is 80,000 dollars a year of owner-paid NOI. At a hypothetical capitalisation rate of 6 percent, that is about 1,333,000 dollars of value, created mostly with lines on a plan drawn before anything was built. If Layout B also costs an extra 200,000 dollars in construction, it is still worth more than six times its cost.

Say that out loud now.

The cheapest operating cost is the one the design made unnecessary.

Worked example: the elevator contract

Elevators are usually maintained under a contract with the installer or an independent firm. Two common forms exist as commercial practice. A full-service contract covers routine maintenance and most repairs and parts for a fixed fee. A parts-and-labour or examination-only contract costs less each year but leaves repairs to be billed separately. Read what is excluded: major components, modernisation and damage are often outside even a full-service contract.

Hypothetical. Two cars on a full-service contract at 12,000 dollars per car per year: 24,000 dollars. An examination-only contract at 6,000 dollars per car: 12,000 dollars, plus repairs averaging, say, 15,000 dollars a year once the equipment ages. The cheaper contract costs more by year eight and transfers the risk of a bad year to you. There is no universal right answer; there is a right answer for your hold period and your appetite for a volatile repairs line.

Also check the term and renewal. Some elevator contracts run for years and renew automatically. A buyer will read that clause, and so should you before you sign it at handover.

Acoustics and vacancy

Noise does not appear as a line in the budget. It appears as turnover. A tenant who hears a neighbour through the floor leaves at the end of the lease, and each turnover costs vacancy, cleaning, marketing and leasing commission. Suppose, hypothetically, poor floor separation adds 10 extra move-outs a year in a 150-unit building, each costing 3,000 dollars all-in. That is 30,000 dollars a year of lost NOI, about 500,000 dollars of value at 6 percent, against an acoustic underlay that would have cost a fraction of that at construction. The hard part is that you never see this number directly; you have to estimate it, and a buyer's analyst will look for it in your turnover rate.

Water and pumping

Water services cost money in three quieter places. Booster pumps run every hour, so their energy depends on how well the system is zoned and controlled; variable-speed pumps that match demand usually cost less to run than fixed-speed pumps throttled by valves. Storage tanks need cleaning and inspection, and Rule 106 adds the cost of a water management plan, its testing and its records. And where an authority limits stormwater release, the detention tank or basin needs inspection and cleaning too. None of these is large on its own. Together they are a recurring line that a buyer's analyst will want to see priced, and that you should price before you choose the system.

Warrick's Wealth Ledger

On your personal balance sheet, every long service contract is a fixed claim on the building's cash, and every ageing elevator or pump set is a capital call waiting to happen. When you hold an asset, list its service contracts with their terms and renewal dates beside its debt maturities, because both are commitments that outlast your attention. And remember that design choices which lower operating cost raise value for as long as you hold, and again when you sell. A licensed adviser is required before you act on any personal wealth decision.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is signing services contracts at handover in a rush, with automatic renewals and exclusions nobody read, and locking the building into costs a buyer will discount. The control is a contract register at handover: every service contract, its scope, exclusions, term, renewal and notice date, reviewed before signature.

The beginner's mistake

Treating security as a staffing line to be cut later. Once the building is laid out badly, the staff are the only control left, and cutting them is a liability decision, not a saving.

Professional sign-off required: security consultant on layout and staffing; elevator consultant on contract scope; accountant on capitalisation and expense treatment.

Callback

In Week 12, I taught capitalised costs and owner accounting. The same distinction runs through services: a contract is an expense, a modernisation is an asset. Classifying them correctly keeps your NOI honest and your depreciation right, and it is the first thing a buyer's accountant will test.

Recap

Services cost money through contracts, energy and staff, and through vacancy when they fail. Good design can remove whole cost lines, as security layout and acoustic separation show. Read every service contract's scope, exclusions and renewal before you sign. Keep a contract register beside your debt maturities.

Next: Ivo, on The Rules: ASME A17.1 for elevators, and the codes for water, waste, stormwater and sound.
checklist: I know which services costs are operating expenses and which are capital.
I have compared design-led and staffing-led security over the hold period.
I have read the scope, exclusions and renewal of every service contract.
A contract register sits beside my debt maturities.
I have estimated the turnover cost of poor acoustics.
In a condominium, I know what services design does to common charges.
Major replacements are in the reserve schedule.
head: Field checklist
speak: Every building service is a subscription I sign at design and pay until I sell. Service contracts, energy and staff are operating expenses before net operating income. Major replacements, such as an elevator modernisation, are usually capitalised, depending on the accounting and tax rules. In a condominium the same costs become common charges that the buyers inherit. Design can remove whole cost lines. A hypothetical lobby laid out with clear sight lines, one controlled entrance and good lighting can cut a round-the-clock guard to evening cover, saving 80,000 dollars a year, worth about 1.3 million dollars at a 6 percent cap rate. Elevator contracts differ in what they cover, and cheaper ones can cost more once equipment ages. Poor acoustics show up as turnover, not as a budget line. I keep a register of every service contract, with exclusions and renewal dates, beside my debt maturities.
terms: Full-service contract — a maintenance contract covering routine service and most repairs and parts for a fixed fee, subject to stated exclusions.
Common charges — the monthly fees condominium owners pay to fund the association's shared operating costs and reserves.
Contract register — a schedule of every service contract with its scope, exclusions, term, renewal and notice dates.

hostile.q: You budget only an evening guard. Is that a real saving, or are you just cutting security to make the numbers work?
hostile.a: It is a design saving, not a cut. Our security consultant reviewed the layout: one controlled entrance with sight lines from the street, the mail room at the entrance, the parking door visible from the desk, lighting to their standard, and access control with cameras on a service contract. On that layout the consultant recommends evening staffing. I have the consultant's report and the cost comparison, and the access-control contract is in our register with its scope and renewal date.

title: Who Governs the Lift, the Pipe, the Rain and the Lock
summary: Elevators follow ASME A17.1 as adopted by a state or city, with their own inspectors and permits. Plumbing, stormwater and sound separation each have their own rules and enforcers. The sharpest conflict this week is between security and egress: a lock may never trap a person the building code says must be able to get out.
body:
Building services are governed by a patchwork: an elevator code with its own inspectors, a plumbing code, a stormwater regime that may involve federal and local permits, sound ratings in the building code, and fire and egress rules that override security. Know who enforces each, and never let a lock beat an exit.

Recall

Q. What is a full-service elevator contract?

A. A maintenance contract covering routine service and most repairs and parts for a fixed fee, subject to stated exclusions such as modernisation or damage. Its form is commercial practice.

Q. Name the three tiers of backup power under the National Electrical Code.

A. Emergency, legally required standby and optional standby, each with its own rules on separation, transfer and testing.

Q. What is a consultant scope gap in design management?

A. A task that falls between two consultants' appointments, so that each assumes the other is doing it and nobody is.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, services are where approvals fragment. Your building permit may be issued by one office, your elevator permit by a state board, your stormwater permit by an environmental agency, and your backflow testing overseen by the water utility. Each can hold up occupancy. Each must be planned as its own approval track. As always this week: verify every requirement against the current adopted edition and local amendments.

Elevators: a code and an inspector of their own

In plain English: an elevator is treated almost like a separate machine that happens to live in your building, with its own safety code, its own permit and its own inspector.

The professional framing is ASME A17.1, the Safety Code for Elevators and Escalators, which covers design, construction, installation, operation, inspection, testing, maintenance and alteration. It is adopted by states and cities, often with a separate elevator authority that issues installation permits, witnesses acceptance tests before the car carries the public, and requires periodic inspections and tests for the life of the equipment. A companion standard, ASME A17.6, covers suspension means such as ropes and belts. The building code then adds what it needs: elevators as part of an accessible route, car sizes that can carry a stretcher in many buildings, and fire service access and occupant evacuation elevators in taller buildings, at thresholds the adopted code sets [unverified — confirm independently].

A worked example, hypothetical. A mid-rise building completes its fit-out. The building inspector is satisfied, but the elevator acceptance test is booked with the state inspector three weeks out. Without a passed acceptance test, the elevator cannot carry the public, and without the elevator the upper floors may not be occupied. A three-week gap has appeared in the critical path from an approval track nobody scheduled. The control is to put the elevator authority's dates on the programme from the day the elevator contract is let.

The code follows the elevator for life. Periodic inspections and tests, at intervals the adopted code and the authority set, are the owner's duty, usually delivered through the maintenance contractor. And an alteration, such as a modernisation of controls or a new door operator, can bring parts of the equipment up to the code edition in force at the time of the work rather than the one it was installed under. So the cost of a future modernisation is partly a code question. When you buy an existing building, ask for the elevator inspection certificates, the last test reports and any outstanding violations, because those transfer with the building and become your problem the day you close.

Water, waste and the public supply

The plumbing code, commonly the International Plumbing Code or the Uniform Plumbing Code as adopted, sets the minimum number of fixtures for an occupancy, methods for sizing water supply and drainage, venting, water heater safety and protection against cross-connection, which is any link through which contaminated water could flow back into the drinking supply. Backflow preventers often require annual testing by a certified tester, with records sent to the water utility; the utility's own rules may be stricter than the code. Verify against the primary source.

Stormwater has two phases. During construction, in the United States, large disturbed sites generally need coverage under a stormwater permit issued under the federal Clean Water Act framework, administered by the Environmental Protection Agency or a delegated state, with a pollution prevention plan for the site. After construction, local ordinances commonly limit the rate and sometimes the quality of runoff, which drives detention and treatment design. Ravi will cover the site side in Week 109.

Say that out loud now.

Each service has its own approval track. If it is not on the programme, it will appear on the critical path.

Sound, light and the energy code

Acoustic separation between dwelling units is a code requirement, not a preference. The building code sets minimum ratings for airborne sound through walls and floors, the sound transmission class, and for impact sound through floors, the impact insulation class, commonly at a rating of 50 for each [unverified — confirm independently]. The ratings apply to tested or listed assemblies, and some jurisdictions allow field testing to confirm them. The commercial point is that the code minimum is a floor; a hospitality brand or a premium condominium may promise more.

Lighting is regulated mainly through the energy code, which limits lighting power density and requires controls such as occupancy sensors and daylight response in many spaces, and through the egress rules, which require illumination of the means of egress. Week 107 covers the energy code in full.

Security versus egress

Here is the conflict to remember. Security wants doors locked; the building and fire codes want people to get out. Wherever the code requires a door to be part of the means of egress, it must be openable from the egress side without a key, special knowledge or effort beyond what the code permits. The codes do allow controlled solutions, such as delayed-egress locking, sensor-release electric locks and access-controlled egress doors, each with conditions such as release on fire alarm activation or loss of power, signage and, sometimes, a sprinklered building. Which ones are permitted in your occupancy is a code question for the adopted edition.

A second worked example, hypothetical. The security consultant proposes magnetic locks on the stair doors at every floor to stop residents roaming the building. Cyrus, from Week 101, would ask: are those stair doors part of the exit route, and do the locks release on fire alarm, on loss of power and from the stair side as the code demands? If the answer is uncertain, the design is wrong until it is certain. A security incident is a liability. A person trapped in a stairwell during a fire is a catastrophe.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is an approval track nobody scheduled, the elevator acceptance test, the backflow certification or the stormwater close-out, holding occupancy after everything else is complete. The control is an approvals register for services, with each authority, each permit, each test and its lead time on the programme.

The beginner's mistake

Letting the security consultant specify locking hardware without a code review. Security and egress must be designed together, and egress wins every conflict.

Professional sign-off required: elevator consultant and the elevator authority; licensed plumbing engineer; civil engineer for stormwater; acoustic consultant; code consultant or fire protection engineer for locking on egress doors.

Callback

In Week 32, Pax and REGA taught entitlements as a sequence of approvals, each with conditions. Services approvals are the same discipline late in the project: separate authorities, separate conditions, separate lead times. The developer who treated entitlements as a programme should treat the elevator, plumbing and stormwater approvals the same way.

Recap

Elevators follow ASME A17.1 as adopted, with their own permits and inspectors. Plumbing codes protect the public supply through backflow rules the utility may enforce. Stormwater has construction and permanent regimes. Sound ratings between homes are code minimums. Security locking must never defeat egress.

Next: Felix, on The Numbers: working backward from a required outage to the water tank and pumps, and from a release limit to a stormwater tank.
checklist: I have an approvals register for elevators, plumbing, backflow and stormwater.
Elevator acceptance test dates are on the programme from contract award.
Backflow testing and reporting duties to the utility are assigned.
Construction stormwater permit coverage has been confirmed.
Permanent stormwater release limits are known and designed for.
Acoustic assemblies meet the adopted ratings, and the brand's promise if higher.
Every lock on an egress door has been reviewed against the code.
head: Field checklist
speak: Building services are governed by a patchwork. Elevators follow ASME A17.1, adopted by states and cities, usually with their own permit and inspector who must witness an acceptance test before the public rides. That test belongs on the programme from day one, or it becomes the critical path. The plumbing code sets fixture counts, sizing, venting and backflow protection, and the water utility may require annual backflow testing. Stormwater has a construction permit regime under the federal Clean Water Act framework and local limits on permanent runoff. The building code sets minimum sound ratings between homes. Lighting is mainly governed by the energy code and egress illumination. The sharpest conflict is security against egress: a door on an exit route must open from the egress side as the code requires, and any special locking needs code conditions such as release on alarm. Egress wins every conflict.
terms: Acceptance test — the inspection and test an elevator must pass, witnessed by the authority, before it may carry the public.
Cross-connection — any link through which contaminated water could flow back into the drinking water supply.
Delayed-egress lock — a locking device permitted by code in some occupancies that holds an exit door for a short, controlled period, subject to release on alarm and other conditions.

hostile.q: Your building is finished and the elevator still cannot run. Why did you not see this coming?
hostile.a: We did see it; the acceptance test date was on our approvals register from contract award, but the authority moved it. We have the inspector's confirmed date, the contractor has the pre-test checks done, and we have asked whether a partial occupancy of the lower floors is possible in the meantime. The lesson I have already taken is to book the test earlier and hold a backup date, and that is now in our standard programme.

title: Working Backward: From a Required Outage to a Tank, and From a Release Limit to a Basin
summary: Two reverse-engineering calculations. Start from a decision, such as surviving a 24-hour water interruption, and work back to tank volume, weight and pump power. Then start from an authority's stormwater release limit and work back to the storage you must build. All numbers are hypothetical and simplified.
body:
Services sizing is best done backward. Decide the outcome you need, a day of water during a supply failure or a release rate the authority will accept, and the arithmetic tells you the tank, the pump and the space, before anyone draws them.

Recall

Q. Why must the elevator acceptance test be on the programme from contract award?

A. Because the elevator authority witnesses it on its own schedule, and without it the elevator cannot carry the public, which can hold occupancy of the upper floors.

Q. What is condensate, and why does it matter?

A. Water removed from air as it is cooled below its dew point. In a humid climate it is a large daily flow that the plumbing must drain, and sometimes it can be reused.

Q. What does a design brief do in design management?

A. It states what the building must achieve, for whom, within what budget and programme, so that every later design decision can be tested against it.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, on an even week we reverse engineer. Most owners receive a tank size and a pump schedule and accept them. Working backward from the outcome lets you see what your decision on autonomy costs in volume, weight, space and water quality, and what a stormwater limit costs in buried concrete. Every figure here is hypothetical and simplified. The engineers of record use the methods and data the adopted codes and the authority require.

Reverse 1: a day of water

The finished outcome you want: a 150-unit residential building that can keep running for 24 hours if the public supply fails.

Step 1, daily demand. Assume a hypothetical 2.5 people per unit and 200 litres per person per day. 150 times 2.5 is 375 people. 375 times 200 is 75,000 litres, which is 75 cubic metres a day.

Step 2, usable versus nominal volume. A tank cannot be drained to the last drop; the outlet sits above the floor and the pumps need a minimum level. Assume 80 percent of the volume is usable. 75 divided by 0.8 is about 94 cubic metres of tank.

Step 3, weight. One cubic metre of water weighs about one tonne. A 94 cubic metre tank holds about 94 tonnes of water, plus the tank itself. If it sits on the roof, Bram's structure must carry it; on the ground, it needs a plant room with a drain and access for cleaning.

Step 4, water quality. At 75 cubic metres a day, the tank turns over roughly once a day, which helps keep water from sitting still. Now change the decision to three days of autonomy. Usable volume becomes 225 cubic metres, nominal about 281 cubic metres, and 281 tonnes of water. Worse, the water now turns over only every three days on average. Day 2's case taught what still water can grow. A larger tank buys resilience and costs both structure and water quality, which means more circulation, treatment and testing under the water management plan.

Step 5, the pump. Assume a hypothetical peak flow of 5 litres per second. The pump must lift water about 40 metres to the top floor, deliver about 20 metres of residual pressure at the highest fixture, and overcome about 10 metres of friction in the pipes: 70 metres of head in total. Hydraulic power is water density times gravity times flow times head: 1,000 kilograms per cubic metre times 9.81 times 0.005 cubic metres per second times 70 metres, which is about 3,400 watts. At a hypothetical pump efficiency of 65 percent, the motor draws about 5.3 kilowatts. Two pumps, each able to carry the load, give a duty and a standby. And if the water must flow during a power outage too, those 5.3 kilowatts go on last week's critical-loads list.

Say that out loud now.

Autonomy costs volume, weight and water quality. I choose the number of hours on purpose, and I price all three.

Reverse 2: from a release limit to a basin

The finished outcome the authority demands: the site may release no more than 20 litres per second of stormwater during the design storm.

Step 1, the runoff. Assume roofs and paving of 4,000 square metres and a hypothetical design storm of 50 millimetres of rain in one hour. Hard surfaces shed most of it; assume a runoff coefficient of 0.9. Volume is area times depth times coefficient: 4,000 times 0.05 metres times 0.9, which is 180 cubic metres in the hour. That is an average inflow of 50 litres per second.

Step 2, what may leave. At 20 litres per second for 3,600 seconds, 72 cubic metres may leave during the storm.

Step 3, what must be held. 180 minus 72 is 108 cubic metres to store and release slowly afterwards. That is the order of magnitude of your detention tank or basin. A real design routes a storm hydrograph through the storage, and the peak can be sharper than an hourly average, so the engineer's figure may be larger.

Step 4, reduce the problem at source. Replace 1,000 square metres of paving with landscape that absorbs water, with a hypothetical runoff coefficient of 0.3, and the runoff falls to 3,000 times 0.05 times 0.9 plus 1,000 times 0.05 times 0.3, which is 135 plus 15, or 150 cubic metres. Storage falls to about 78 cubic metres. A green roof or permeable paving can do similar work. Each choice trades construction cost and maintenance against buried concrete.

What the numbers buy in space

Turn both answers into floor area, because space is what you will lose at a stage gate. A 94 cubic metre tank, 2.5 metres deep, needs about 38 square metres of footprint before access and pumps; call it 50 square metres of plant room. A 108 cubic metre detention tank at a similar depth needs about 43 square metres below ground, which may sit under parking or landscape but must stay accessible for cleaning. Together, nearly 100 square metres of the site and the building are spoken for by two decisions you can now explain in a sentence each. Put both on Day 1's space allocation sheet, signed, before the architect fills that area with something that earns rent.

Checking the engineer's numbers

Your rough numbers are questions. If the tank on the drawings is three times your figure, ask what demand rate, autonomy and fire-fighting storage were assumed, because some buildings must also hold water for fire protection, which Magnus covered in Week 102. If the detention tank is half your figure, ask what storm and runoff coefficients were used, and whether the authority has confirmed them.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is choosing autonomy by instinct, "more is safer", and ending with a tank that is too heavy, too large to turn over and too expensive to manage. The control is a written autonomy decision, with its volume, weight and water quality consequences shown side by side.

The beginner's mistake

Forgetting that the booster pumps need power. A full tank is useless during an outage if the pumps that lift its water are not on backup power.

Professional sign-off required: licensed plumbing engineer for water storage and pumps; structural engineer for tank loads; civil engineer for stormwater.

Callback

In Week 17, Sage taught reverse engineering a deal from public information to an implied land price. The method is the same here: start from the outcome you can see or must achieve, and work back through each step until the hidden quantity appears. The quantities differ; the discipline does not.

Recap

A 24-hour supply of water for 150 units is about 94 cubic metres of tank and 94 tonnes; three days is about 281 tonnes and slower turnover. The booster set is sized from flow and head and must be on backup power if water must flow in an outage. A release limit works back to detention storage, which source controls can reduce.

Next: Marco, on The Room: the meeting where the services are cut to save money.
checklist: I have decided the water autonomy period in writing.
I know the tank volume, weight and turnover that decision implies.
The structural engineer has the tank load and location.
Booster pumps are duty and standby, and on backup power if needed.
Fire-fighting water storage, if required, is counted separately.
I know the authority's stormwater release limit and design storm.
I have priced source controls against detention storage.
head: Field checklist
speak: I size services backward from the outcome. To keep a hypothetical 150-unit building running for a day without the public supply, I estimate 375 people at 200 litres each, about 75 cubic metres. Only 80 percent of a tank is usable, so I need about 94 cubic metres: 94 tonnes of water the structure must carry, turning over about once a day. Three days of autonomy means about 281 tonnes and water that sits three times as long, which raises the water-quality burden. The booster pump, at a hypothetical 5 litres a second against 70 metres of head, draws about 5.3 kilowatts, so it goes on backup power if water must flow in an outage. For stormwater, 4,000 square metres of hard surface in a 50-millimetre storm sheds 180 cubic metres; at a 20 litres-a-second limit I must hold about 108. Landscape that absorbs water shrinks that.
terms: Autonomy — the length of time a building can keep operating on stored water or fuel after the public supply fails.
Head — the pressure a pump must provide, expressed as the height of water it could lift, including friction losses and required residual pressure.
Runoff coefficient — the fraction of rainfall on a surface that runs off rather than soaking in.

hostile.q: Your tank is sized for one day. Wouldn't three days be safer for the residents?
hostile.a: Safer for supply, worse for water quality and structure. Three days triples the volume to about 281 tonnes and means water sits three times as long, which our water management plan would then have to fight with circulation and treatment. We chose one day because the utility's record shows interruptions shorter than that, the booster pumps are on backup power, and we have a written plan for water delivery if an outage runs longer. I can show you the comparison.

title: The Cost Meeting Where the Second Elevator Disappears
summary: The estimate is over budget and the quickest savings look invisible: one elevator instead of two, a thinner acoustic underlay, a smaller water tank, a cheaper lobby. Each one quietly removes something occupants will notice. Learn to run the meeting so every cut is judged against the requirements you wrote, not against the budget alone.
body:
Services cuts are tempting because they are invisible on the drawings and obvious in the building. Run the meeting against your written requirements, separate the cuts that remove cost from the cuts that remove function, and make the hard choices in daylight with your name on them.

Recall

Q. What does three days of water autonomy cost compared with one?

A. About three times the volume and weight, and water that turns over three times more slowly, which raises the water-quality burden under the water management plan.

Q. What is the standing rule for MEP value engineering?

A. No item is accepted in the meeting where it is first proposed; each is converted into capital, operating and reserve numbers and the critical-loads answer, and decided later.

Q. What is the difference between interests and positions in negotiation?

A. A position is what someone says they want; an interest is why they want it. Solving for interests often finds an option neither side's position would have reached.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, I will chair this meeting as your owner's project manager, and you will make the decisions. The pattern is common: an estimate arrives over budget late in design, and the services list offers savings that seem painless because nobody can see an elevator that was never built. The cost of those savings arrives after handover, as complaints, turnover and a reputation you cannot quickly repair.

The scene

This is a composite scene with hypothetical numbers. Present: you, me, the architect, the cost consultant, Felix for services, Noor for acoustics and Silas for security. The estimate is 1,200,000 dollars over. The cost consultant presents a list: delete the second elevator, 350,000 dollars; replace the floor acoustic underlay with a thinner product, 180,000 dollars; reduce the water tank from one day to half a day, 60,000 dollars; drop the lobby re-planning that opened sight lines to the parking entrance, 90,000 dollars; reduce corridor lighting levels and fixtures, 70,000 dollars; and a long list of finishes and fittings making up the rest.

The architect adds, kindly, "None of these affects the code compliance."

The lines to say

Open by separating two kinds of cut. "Thank you. I want to split this list into two columns. Column one removes cost and keeps function. Column two removes function. We can move quickly on column one today. Column two we judge against the requirements document, one item at a time."

Then ask each specialist one question, by name. "Felix, with one elevator, what is the peak wait, and what happens to an upper-floor resident in a wheelchair when the only car is out for service?" "Noor, does the thinner underlay meet our requirement, which is above the code minimum because we promised quiet homes in the sales material?" "Silas, if we drop the lobby changes, what does your staffing recommendation become?"

Each answer converts a hidden cost into a visible one. Felix: the wait doubles at peak, and one car out means the stairs for everyone. Noor: the thinner product meets the code rating on paper but not our requirement, and impact noise is the most common complaint in this building type. Silas: without the sight lines, the evening desk becomes a round-the-clock desk, which Nadia priced on Day 3 at about 80,000 dollars a year more.

Then the sentence that keeps you honest: "If we take any column-two item, I will sign it with its consequence written beside it, and we will check whether any sales or leasing material promised the thing we are removing."

Say that out loud now.

Which of these removes cost, and which removes function?

The lines never to say

Never say "nobody will notice". Residents notice elevators, noise and dark corridors within a week, and buyers' lawyers notice promises in sales material.

Never say "it meets code, so it is fine". The code is a floor for safety and health, not a description of the product you are selling. Day 4 showed that the code's sound rating is a minimum, and Week 105 showed that the code's backup power list may not match your occupants.

Never let the cost consultant own the decision. The consultant prices options. You choose them.

The question behind the question

Why are services first on the list? Often because the cost consultant needs a large, quick number, and services items are large and look technical enough that nobody will argue. Sometimes the real overrun is elsewhere, in the structure, the façade or an escalation allowance that was too thin, and the services cut is papering over it. Ask, calmly, "Where did the overrun come from, line by line, since the last estimate?" If the answer is the façade, the right conversation is about the façade.

When to stay silent

After each specialist answers, say nothing for a few seconds. Let the consequence sit in the room. The architect may offer an alternative: perhaps the second elevator can be a smaller car in the same shaft size, at a lower cost. That kind of idea only appears when nobody rushes to fill the silence with a decision.

How to hold your state

Over-budget meetings produce a specific pressure: the wish to be seen fixing it. Notice it. Keep your voice slow. Remember that you are not choosing between the budget and the building; you are choosing which of several real costs to carry, and when. If you feel rushed, use the sentence you learned last week: "Noted. We decide on Thursday."

Two worked outcomes

Hypothetical. Column one, the finishes and fittings, delivers 650,000 dollars today with no loss of function. Of column two, you accept the corridor lighting change after Noor shows a fixture layout that meets the requirement with fewer, better-placed fittings: 50,000 dollars. You keep the second elevator but accept a smaller car in the same shaft: 120,000 dollars saved. You keep the underlay and the lobby planning, because each saves less than the operating cost or turnover it creates. You decline the tank cut, because half a day of water fails your written autonomy decision.

That totals 820,000 dollars. The remaining 380,000 dollars you take to the structure and façade overrun, where it started, and to a contingency drawdown you approve in writing. The budget is closed without removing anything occupants will feel.

The second outcome is worth rehearsing too. Suppose nothing else can be found and you must cut a function. Then you choose the one whose consequence is most reversible later, record why, and tell your lender, investors and sales team before they discover it.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is removing a function that sales material, a brand standard or a lease promised, and turning a cost saving into a misrepresentation claim. The control is a check of every column-two item against marketing, leasing and brand commitments before it is accepted.

The beginner's mistake

Treating the cost consultant's list as a menu to pick from to hit a number. The professional treats it as a set of options to test against requirements, and goes back to find where the overrun really came from.

Professional sign-off required: elevator consultant; acoustic consultant; security consultant; legal counsel where a cut may contradict sales or leasing material.

Callback

In Week 51, Quincy and Nadia taught contingency structure and cost-to-complete. An over-budget estimate in design is the moment to ask whether the contingency was right, not only what to cut. Sometimes the honest answer is a controlled contingency drawdown, recorded and reported, rather than a hidden loss of function.

Recap

Split cuts into those that remove cost and those that remove function. Ask each specialist the consequence by name. Find where the overrun came from. Check every function cut against sales, leasing and brand commitments. Decide column-two items later, in writing, with the consequence beside your signature.

Next: Kema, on Quiz and Recap: six questions on building services, a Red Pen drill and the boardroom drill.
checklist: I split every cost list into cuts that remove cost and cuts that remove function.
I ask each specialist the consequence of a cut, by name, in the room.
I ask where the overrun came from, line by line.
I check function cuts against sales, leasing and brand commitments.
I do not accept 'it meets code' as a reason to remove a promised function.
Every accepted function cut is signed with its consequence written beside it.
I tell my lender, investors and sales team before they discover a cut.
head: Field checklist
speak: When an estimate comes in over budget, the services list offers savings that look invisible: one elevator instead of two, a thinner acoustic underlay, a smaller water tank, a cheaper lobby. I start by splitting the list into two columns: cuts that remove cost and keep function, and cuts that remove function. Column one we can take quickly. Column two I judge against the requirements I wrote, one item at a time. I ask each specialist the consequence by name: the elevator wait, the noise rating against what we promised, the extra security staffing. I ask where the overrun actually came from, because the services cut may be papering over a façade or structure problem. I never say nobody will notice, and I never accept 'it meets code' as the reason. I check every function cut against sales and leasing promises, and I sign it with its consequence beside my name.
terms: Owner's project manager — the professional who runs the project on the owner's behalf, chairing meetings and managing consultants and contractors.
Function cut — a saving that removes something occupants will experience, as distinct from one that only lowers cost.
Contingency drawdown — an approved, recorded use of the project's contingency to cover a cost increase.

hostile.q: You found 820,000 dollars and still drew on contingency. Why didn't you just delete the second elevator and keep the contingency intact?
hostile.a: Because the second elevator removes function residents will feel within a week, and with one car an upper-floor resident in a wheelchair has no access when it is out for service. We took 120,000 dollars by using a smaller car in the same shaft. The overrun came from the façade and structure, so the contingency drawdown is where the cost originated, approved in writing and reported to you. Our sales material also promised two elevators, which made deleting one a legal question as well.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Building Services in Review: Space, Water, Lifts and the Lock That Must Open
summary: Six questions on water, waste, elevators, sound, light and security, a Red Pen drill on a hypothetical services memo, and a two-minute boardroom drill. Answer each question aloud before reading the answer.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: occupants judge the building by its services, every service needs space and a route decided early, and the hazards hidden in water, lifts and locks must be managed in writing by the owner.

Recall

Q. In the cost meeting, what are the two columns?

A. Cuts that remove cost and keep function, which can be taken quickly, and cuts that remove function, which are judged one by one against the written requirements and any sales, leasing or brand commitments.

Q. What is a dedicated outdoor air system for?

A. Drying and conditioning all incoming fresh air centrally, so room units only handle heat, which is the main defence against damp rooms in a humid climate.

Q. What does a structure peer review protect against?

A. One engineering firm's blind spot becoming the building's weakness, by having an independent engineer check the design basis, loads and key elements.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, building services are where small decisions produce daily experiences for every occupant. If you can answer these six questions without notes, you can defend services space at a stage gate and run a cost meeting without losing the building. Answer each aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. Why does every building service need space decided early?

Answer: Because tanks, plant rooms, risers, shafts and ceiling voids look like empty area at concept and are the first space lost to rentable area. Once the structure and core are fixed, adding them back is expensive or impossible. A signed space allocation sheet per service protects them.

Question 2. What is CPTED, and why does it come before cameras?

Answer: Crime prevention through environmental design: sight lines, lighting, clear boundaries and natural surveillance that make a space feel watched and owned. It comes first because a well-planned layout reduces the need for staff and technology, which then support a design that already works.

Question 3. What is Rule 106?

Answer: Every water system in a building you own gets a written water management plan, with a named owner, monitoring and response triggers; warm or stagnant water is a hazard to manage, never a reserve to forget.

Question 4. Who governs elevators, and what must happen before one carries the public?

Answer: ASME A17.1, adopted by a state or city, usually enforced by a separate elevator authority. The elevator must pass an acceptance test witnessed by that authority, and then periodic inspections and tests for life.

Question 5. Where does security conflict with the code, and which wins?

Answer: At doors on the means of egress. Security wants them locked; the codes require them to open from the egress side as specified, with special locking allowed only under code conditions such as release on fire alarm. Egress wins every conflict.

Question 6. What does a choice of water autonomy cost?

Answer: Volume, weight and water quality. Each extra day multiplies tank size and structural load and slows turnover, which increases the treatment and testing needed. The booster pumps must also be on backup power if water must flow in an outage.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Felix, Noor and Silas set the frame: water, waste, stormwater, elevators, lighting, acoustics and security, each needing space early. Ford took the 2015 South Bronx Legionnaires' outbreak, traced to a cooling tower, giving Rule 106. Nadia showed services as a subscription and priced security by design against security by staffing. Ivo mapped the approval tracks and the security-egress conflict. Felix worked backward from autonomy to a tank and from a release limit to a basin. Marco ran the cost meeting where the second elevator nearly disappeared.

Red Pen drill

Read this hypothetical services memo and find the defects before reading on.

Services Summary. Water: three days of storage provided on the roof for maximum resilience; booster pumps are a single duty pump to save cost; pumps on normal power only. Water treatment to be handled by the maintenance contractor; no further plan required. Elevators: one passenger elevator, which meets code; acceptance testing to be arranged near completion. Acoustics: floors meet the code minimum rating; marketing materials describe "whisper-quiet homes". Security: magnetic locks on all stair doors at every floor to keep the stairs secure. Stormwater: detention to be designed after the authority comments.

The defects. First, three days of roof storage triples the structural load and slows turnover, with no note of either consequence or of Bram's review. Second, a single pump is a single point of failure; there is no standby. Third, pumps on normal power mean the stored water cannot reach upper floors in an outage, which defeats the purpose of storage. Fourth, "no further plan required" for water treatment breaks Rule 106. Fifth, one elevator meets code but has no redundancy for residents who cannot use stairs, and there is no traffic analysis. Sixth, acceptance testing "near completion" invites a gap on the critical path. Seventh, code-minimum floors beside a "whisper-quiet" promise is a misrepresentation risk. Eighth, magnetic locks on stair doors need a code review for egress release; as written they may trap people. Ninth, stormwater designed only after authority comments means the release limit and storage space were never protected.

The boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes, as if to an investor who asks, "Why does your services budget look generous?" Then compare with this model.

Model answer: "Because services are what residents judge us by every day, and fixing them after handover costs far more than getting them right now. We sized water storage for one day, which turns over daily and keeps water quality manageable, with duty and standby pumps on backup power. Every water system has a written management plan, with monthly readings to me. We have two elevators so nobody is stranded when one is serviced, and the acceptance test is on the programme now. Floors exceed the code minimum because we promised quiet homes. The lobby is planned for sight lines, which cuts security staffing to evening cover and saves more each year than the design cost. Stair locks release as the code requires. When the estimate went over, we cut cost, not function, and traced the overrun to where it began."

Score your answer. Did you open with the bottom line? Did you name at least one hazard and its control? Did you connect a design choice to operating cost? Did you finish inside two minutes? If not, record it again tomorrow.

Then try the hard follow-up an investor often asks next: "What would you cut first if you had to?" A strong answer names a column-one item, such as a finish or a fitting, and explains why it removes cost without removing function. A weak answer names the second elevator or the acoustic underlay, because it shows you have not yet separated the two columns in your own head. Practise saying, in one sentence, which items you would never cut and why: the standby pump, the water management plan and the egress release on the stair locks. Those three protect people, not comfort, and an investor who hears you say so calmly learns how you will behave when the next estimate arrives over budget.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is that invisible services decisions, an omitted pump, an unscheduled approval, a lock without a code review, become visible only when occupants are already inside. The control is the trio of documents you now own: the space allocation sheets, the approvals register and the water management plan.

The beginner's mistake

Confusing "meets code" with "meets our promise". The code protects safety and health; your sales and leasing material defines the product.

Callback

In Week 98, Zara and Cade taught consultant scopes and the gaps between them. The Red Pen memo is full of gaps: water treatment left to a contractor, stormwater deferred, locking specified by security alone. Every one is a scope gap waiting to become a defect.

Recap

Protect services space at concept. Size water autonomy on purpose and manage the water in writing. Schedule every approval track. Design security around egress, never against it. Cut cost, not function, and check every cut against your promises.

head: The six questions
speak: This week, building services. Occupants judge a building by its water pressure, drains, elevators, quiet and sense of safety, and every one needs space and a route decided at concept. I size water storage for a chosen autonomy, knowing each extra day adds volume, weight and stagnant water, and I put duty and standby booster pumps on backup power. The 2015 South Bronx Legionnaires' outbreak, traced to a cooling tower, gives Rule 106: every water system gets a written water management plan with an owner, monitoring and triggers. Elevators follow ASME A17.1 as adopted, with an acceptance test that belongs on the programme from day one. Sound ratings are code minimums, and my promises may be higher. Security starts with sight lines and lighting, and egress wins every conflict with a lock. When costs run over, I cut cost, not function.
terms: Space allocation sheet — a signed record of the space a building service needs and the design stage by which it must be confirmed.
Approvals register — a schedule of every permit, inspection and test a project needs, with the authority, lead time and status.
Single point of failure — one component whose failure stops a whole service, such as a single pump or a single elevator.

hostile.q: The code allows one elevator and a single pump. Why are you spending more than the code requires?
hostile.a: Because the code sets a minimum for safety, not for service. A single pump or a single elevator is a single point of failure: when it is out, upper floors lose water or access, and some residents cannot use stairs. The duty and standby pumps and the second car are priced, the space was protected at concept, and our sales material promised the service level they deliver. Deleting them would save money once and cost us in complaints, turnover and possibly claims for years.
